source.name: ASTRA Bio wave 1 — Transport in Plants
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: Passive movement of a solute from higher to lower concentration without a carrier is
questions.explanation: Simple diffusion is downhill and carrier-independent; facilitated diffusion still needs a protein but no ATP.

questions.stem: Uphill pumping of mineral ions across a membrane with expenditure of ATP is
questions.explanation: Active transport uses metabolic energy to move solutes against their electrochemical gradient.

questions.stem: Water potential of a plant cell is the algebraic sum of
options: only gravitational potential of the soil
questions.explanation: ψw = ψs + ψp (plus a small gravity term in tall columns); solute potential is negative.

questions.stem: Shrinkage of the protoplast from the cell wall after a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution is
questions.explanation: Hypertonic external solution draws water out; the protoplast pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis).

questions.stem: Water moving through cell walls and intercellular spaces without crossing the plasma membrane follows the
questions.explanation: The apoplast is the non-living wall continuum; the symplast is the cytoplasm linked by plasmodesmata.

questions.stem: Loss of water vapour from aerial plant parts, mainly through stomata, is
questions.explanation: Transpiration is evaporative loss; stomatal transpiration accounts for most of it in land plants.

questions.stem: Influx of potassium ions into guard cells typically causes stomata to
questions.explanation: K+ uptake lowers guard-cell water potential, water enters, turgor rises and the pore opens.

questions.stem: The cohesion–tension mechanism of ascent of sap was put forward by
questions.explanation: Dixon and Joly explained continuous water columns held by cohesion and pulled by transpiration.

questions.stem: Guttation droplets appear at hydathodes mainly when
options: root pressure is high and transpiration is low
stomata are the only exit and air is very dry
questions.explanation: At night, low transpiration lets root pressure force liquid water out of hydathodes.

questions.stem: The mass-flow (pressure-flow) hypothesis of phloem transport is associated with
questions.explanation: Münch proposed that source loading raises turgor and drives bulk flow toward the sink.

questions.stem: Facilitated diffusion of a polar solute across the plasma membrane requires
options: a membrane protein but no metabolic energy
questions.explanation: Carriers or channels speed downhill movement; the process is passive and saturates.

questions.stem: Casparian strips force inward water movement to switch from the apoplast to the
questions.explanation: Suberised strips block the wall path, so water and ions must cross endodermal membranes.

questions.stem: Choose the correct statements. I. Imbibition is the adsorption of water by hydrophilic colloids such as cellulose. II. A flaccid cell has zero pressure potential. III. Phloem sap always moves only upward from root to leaf.
questions.explanation: Imbibition and ψp = 0 in a flaccid cell are correct; phloem transport is source to sink and can be downward.

questions.stem: Which property is shared by simple diffusion and facilitated diffusion?
options: Both require ATP at the membrane
Both move solutes down a concentration gradient
Both always move water against osmosis
questions.explanation: Both are passive (downhill); only facilitated diffusion uses a specific membrane protein.

questions.stem: A proton pump in the plant plasma membrane is an example of
questions.explanation: H+-ATPases hydrolyse ATP to export protons and build the electrochemical gradient used for secondary transport.

questions.stem: Pure water at atmospheric pressure is assigned a water potential of
questions.explanation: By convention ψw of pure water at standard pressure is zero; solutes make ψs and ψw negative.

questions.stem: Dry seeds swell by taking up water through
questions.explanation: Hydrophilic colloids (cellulose, proteins) imbibe water and generate imbibition pressure.

questions.stem: The symplast pathway of water movement depends on
questions.explanation: Symplastic flow is through living protoplasts connected by plasmodesmata.

questions.stem: Which condition generally lowers the rate of transpiration?
options: high wind speed around the leaf
very high relative humidity of the air
questions.explanation: Humid air reduces the vapour-pressure gradient from the substomatal cavity to the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Abscisic acid accumulated during water stress typically causes stomata to
questions.explanation: ABA triggers K+ efflux from guard cells, turgor falls and the pore closes, saving water.

questions.stem: A continuous water column in xylem is maintained largely by
options: cohesion among water molecules and adhesion to walls
imbibition in the leaf mesophyll only
root pressure throughout a tall tree every noon
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding holds the column together and to lignified walls under transpiration tension.

questions.stem: Root pressure can be demonstrated experimentally as
options: exudation of sap from a freshly cut stump
wilting of a leaf in dry wind
plasmolysis of onion peel in sugar
opening of stomata in darkness only
questions.explanation: A detopped well-watered plant may bleed xylem sap, evidence of positive root pressure.

questions.stem: According to the pressure-flow model, phloem loading at the source
options: lowers turgor so sap is sucked from the sink
raises solute content and turgor, pushing sap toward the sink
questions.explanation: Sugar loading makes ψs more negative, water enters, turgor rises and bulk flow proceeds to the sink.

questions.stem: Which statement about osmosis in plant cells is incorrect?
options: Water moves toward the more negative water potential.
A turgid cell in pure water has high pressure potential.
Solute potential of a solution is usually negative.
A hypertonic external solution always raises the cell’s turgor.
questions.explanation: A hypertonic bath draws water out, so turgor falls and plasmolysis may follow.

questions.stem: Antitranspirants are substances applied to leaves mainly to
options: block phloem loading at the source
questions.explanation: Films or metabolic antitranspirants cut water loss; they are used under water-limited conditions.

questions.stem: Identify the incorrect statement about long-distance transport.
options: Xylem sap is under tension during rapid transpiration.
Root pressure can cause guttation at night.
Phloem translocation is bidirectional in the plant as a whole.
Ascent of sap in tall trees is explained solely by root pressure every afternoon.
questions.explanation: Root pressure is too small and often absent at midday; cohesion–tension accounts for tall-tree ascent.
